claims.text: Adding Nb to HfZrTi will improve its ductility.
Adding Nb to HfZrTi will improve its toughness.
Nb addition will promote a dual-phase microstructure in HfZrTi.
The proposed dual-phase microstructure will enhance dislocation mobility.
The proposed dual-phase microstructure will retard crack propagation.
Standard HfZrTi HEA is generally single-phase.
Standard HfZrTi HEA generally has limited ductility and toughness.
The limited mechanical performance is caused by a homogeneous microstructure lacking efficient carriers of plastic deformation.
Melting or powder metallurgy followed by thermo-mechanical treatment can produce solid-solution formation and a well-dispersed dual-phase microstructure in Nb-modified HfZrTi.
Nb may induce a secondary, more ductile phase in HfZrTi.
Nb may modify the grain-boundary character of HfZrTi.
A secondary ductile phase or modified grain boundaries will provide heterogeneous deformation sites and facilitate stress redistribution.
Niobium has a relatively large atomic size and inherent ductility.
Nb-induced localized lattice distortions will lower energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Lower barriers for dislocation motion will facilitate plastic deformation and delay crack initiation and propagation.
Nb-alloyed HfZrTi should have higher strain to failure than baseline HfZrTi under comparable tests.
Nb-alloyed HfZrTi should have higher fracture energy or toughness than baseline HfZrTi under comparable tests.
Excessive Nb or inappropriate heat treatment may cause phase segregation or embrittlement.
Other HEAs have shown analogous improvements after the addition of ductile alloying elements.
Direct evidence for the HfZrTi-Nb system is limited, and its optimal Nb concentration and processing parameters are undetermined.
